title: Understanding is the new bottleneck
summary: Argues developers must still understand agent-written code in order to participate creatively, and shows explainer docs, quizzes and agent-built micro-worlds as ways to build that understanding quickly.

assertions.quote: Agents are writing more and more code for us, and we all know it's getting harder to keep up.

verdicts.note: DORA and field reports show review and verification load growing with AI output, consistent with instability and persistent-debt findings.

assertions.quote: Hot take: I think it's still important to understand the code that our agents write!

verdicts.note: Ignoring code entirely leads to drift and debt in real codebases; but spec-driven approaches with code review do work.

assertions.quote: It's like tech debt: you can get away with not understanding what's going on in the short term, but it'll bite you eventually.

verdicts.note: Naur's theory-building view and early studies of AI-assisted teams support loss of understanding as a real risk, but there is no measurement yet showing it outweighs technical debt.
Authors conclude that AI-assisted development does not appear to introduce code-level technical debt, and warn that cognitive debt is the greater concern; the warning is not empirically tested here.

Cognitive debt (deferred understanding of accepted code) is reported in 24% (8) of RQ3.1 sources with warnings of long-term unmaintainable systems; the review never compares its size with technical debt.

The study shows only a short-term loss of individual code comprehension right after writing, and it explicitly leaves long-term effects to future work. It makes no comparison with technical debt, so only the mechanism, not the 'bigger risk' ranking, is supported.

assertions.quote: walking through the changes in a sensible order, with surrounding explanation and embedded code snippets. Faster to review than a raw diff.

verdicts.note: Agents do speed onboarding and PR summarization, but surveys and the Anthropic learning study show many users skip understanding; outcome depends on use.

assertions.quote: A quiz is a speed regulator. Working with AI, it's easy for the loop to run faster than the speed of human understanding.

verdicts.note: This is a personal workflow practice drawn from learning-science ideas; its value for code comprehension has not been measured.

Quizzes generated by o1 about the participant's own code exposed a comprehension gap after AI use, so quizzing does reveal lost understanding. The study used quizzes only to measure and did not test whether they help as an intervention; the authors propose active-review mechanisms as future work.

assertions.quote: The point here is that agents can write bits of code that help us humans understand other code.

verdicts.note: Small standalone throwaway tools are where AI generation is most reliable, and many practitioners report building debugging aids they previously skipped.
